title: Overlord
label: Quick read (from summaries)
premise: When the online game YGGDRASIL shuts down, guild leader Momonga stays logged in and finds himself trapped in his skeletal undead avatar in a new world, along with his guild's Great Tomb of Nazarick and its now-living, fanatically loyal NPC servants. Taking the name Ainz Ooal Gown, he explores and expands his power while searching for other players.
life_message: It explores what happens when unchecked power meets a mind that no longer feels ordinary moral limits, largely from the would-be villain's side.

content.note: Battles, war and killing without moral qualms; slavery in the setting (Wikipedia; AniList War, Slavery, Anti-Hero).
Undead and demon characters; cruelty toward humans (AniList Skeleton, Necromancy, Demons; to verify intensity).
Succubus guardian's infatuation with Ainz; some suggestive designs (AniList Succubus; to verify).
Ainz's loss of human emotion is a recurring thread (to verify).
Protagonist kills and deceives freely, which the story attributes to his undead nature (Wikipedia; AniList Anti-Hero).
Video-game framework; wide media franchise including a gacha game (Wikipedia).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Insults to Ainz or Nazarick are met with retribution by his guardians.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Nazarick runs on strict obedience to the supreme being.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty to the guild 'family' over outsiders.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Servants revere Ainz absolutely; strict rank among guardians.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Game logic and calculated strategy guide his decisions.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Security and expansion of Nazarick dominate.

folkways.japan: The guardians' devotion mirrors Japanese ideals of loyal retainers and a company-like chain of command, magnified to absolute obedience.

delivery.evidence: Entry notes irony as the story's only check on Ainz; no review on delivery found (to verify).

personified.ideology: unchecked power without ordinary moral limits

delivery.note: The story is told largely from the would-be villain's side and leaves judgment of his conquests to the reader (to verify).

winners_losers: Ainz and Nazarick keep winning; human kingdoms and adventurers lose. Sympathy goes to Ainz's perspective, with the story's irony as its only check.
